meldungen.titel: Consulting Deep Dive, part 7: Strategy& and the strategy arms of the Big Four, where strategy meets the deal
meldungen.text:
After MBB and the specialist tier, the series turns to a different animal: the strategy houses that sit inside the large audit and advisory networks. Strategy& belongs to PwC, EY-Parthenon to EY, Monitor to Deloitte, and KPMG runs its own strategy group. What unites them is proximity to transactions. They share a roof with the deals, valuation and transaction services teams of their parent, and that shapes both the work and the exits.

Strategy& is the most traditional of the four. It is the former Booz & Company, absorbed by PwC in 2014, and describes itself as PwC's global strategy consulting business with more than 3,000 consultants in over 75 offices. It serves corporate clients and private equity firms alike, including value creation diligence on deals, and in Germany, Austria and Switzerland it recruits all year round rather than in fixed cycles. In the UK, PwC even advertises separate graduate strategy tracks in consulting and in Deals, a neat illustration of how close the two worlds are.

EY-Parthenon makes the same point on its German careers page: its work ranges from classic strategy projects to large M&A transactions and strategic private equity mandates, including due diligence for leading PE clients. In practice this means more commercial due diligence and post-deal work than at a pure strategy firm, often under tight deal timetables. The next instalment looks at commercial due diligence as a speciality in its own right.

On exits, one coaching guide lists eight typical destinations for Strategy& alumni: corporate strategy, private equity value creation, technology, internal moves within PwC, start-ups, general management, public sector advisory and a sponsored MBA. Its verdict is that alumni end up in roughly the same places as MBB alumni, but have to search more deliberately. Two caveats matter. First, a recruiter unfamiliar with consulting may read a Strategy& CV as generic Big Four advisory rather than strategy, so you have to tell the story yourself. Second, most consultants who move into private equity land in value creation, portfolio operations or operating roles at portfolio companies rather than on investment teams. Those seats pay less than the reported average US PE associate salary of about 249,000 dollars, but come with saner hours.

The internal route is the distinctive one. Because the parent firm runs transaction services, valuation and corporate finance under the same brand, a move from strategy into deals work is possible without changing employer, and that experience is exactly what PE funds and corporate development teams ask for in German and Austrian job postings. The flip side: the brand pull of the strategy arm is weaker than that of MBB, and for Deloitte Monitor and KPMG Strategy no reliable exit data turned up in this morning's research, so treat any claims about them with caution.

The long-term picture: Strategy& and EY-Parthenon are a credible door into private equity on the operating side, into corporate M&A and into CFO track roles, particularly if you combine strategy projects with a stint in transaction services. For a large-cap PE deal team, Bain and McKinsey remain the more direct road.

meldungen.titel: An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude have proved the Riemann Hypothesis, and the machine check is holding up
meldungen.text:
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician employed by Anthropic, has announced a possible proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, arguably the most famous open problem in mathematics. He says he found it together with Claude, his employer's model. What makes the claim more than bravado is its form: rather than a conventional paper, Alpöge has published the argument formalised in Lean, a proof assistant that checks every logical step mechanically.

The scale is striking. According to Alpöge, a written exposition that Claude christened the "GRH book" ran to more than 250,000 pages; he judged it unreadable and did not publish it. What exists so far is mainly a large body of Lean code. A human-readable version is promised.

Early independent checks are encouraging. The code compiles without errors and is accepted by two independently developed Lean kernels, and Scientific American reports that independent mathematicians now consider the proof very likely correct. The decisive open question is subtler: a successful formal check only shows that the stated theorems follow from the axioms used. Whether the definitions and the final statement capture the Riemann Hypothesis exactly, without gaps, still has to be confirmed by specialists. The Clay Mathematics Institute continues to list the problem as unsolved, with a one million dollar prize for an accepted solution.

In parallel, a second, entirely human attempt has surfaced. Ravi Vakil, the Stanford mathematician and president of the American Mathematical Society, wrote in a "hasty announcement" on his blog that Alessandro Masullo has proposed a proof of the generalised Riemann Hypothesis, which Brian Conrad has been reviewing for months. Conrad told Scientific American that the manuscript is currently being fundamentally revised. Vakil stressed that Masullo's work was done without AI.

Why it matters: posed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis states that all non-trivial zeros of the zeta function lie on a single line, with real part one half. If true, it pins down the distribution of prime numbers as precisely as is theoretically possible, and countless results in number theory that are currently conditional ("if the Riemann Hypothesis holds") would become theorems overnight. More than ten trillion zeros have been computed, all on the line, but no amount of computation can rule out an exception.

What comes next is the slow part: experts must verify that the Lean statement is the real thing, and Alpöge must deliver a readable proof. If both hold, this would be the first Millennium Problem settled with an AI as co-author.

meldungen.titel: Nvidia under SEC scrutiny drags tech lower, the DAX slips below 25,000 and Bitcoin hits a two-year low
meldungen.text:
The week ended with a broad sell-off in technology and AI stocks on US exchanges, according to Deutschlandfunk, and Europe followed: the DAX fell below 25,000 points. Index trackers felt it directly; Börse Express reported a drop of 3.4 per cent for the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF in the AI sell-off.

At the centre is Nvidia. Its shares fell 14 per cent, the FAZ reports, as the Securities and Exchange Commission investigates. According to the Wall Street Journal, the regulator has opened a civil inquiry into whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors, and California's attorney general is weighing action of his own; neither the SEC nor Nvidia has confirmed the probe. The backdrop is the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang on 12 November, after reports about his ties to a manager at a Singapore company that US intelligence links to Chinese services, and about chips possibly diverted to China. Finance chief Colette Kress is running the company on an interim basis.

The risk-off mood reached crypto as well. Bitcoin fell to around 55,300 dollars, its lowest level since September 2024; the asset manager CoinShares speaks of an "advanced capitulation" and is pinning its hopes on a change of course at the Fed. That hope looks thin for now: markets have almost fully priced in a US rate rise in December, and in the euro area there is speculation about a double tightening by the ECB, a rate step plus higher minimum reserves.

For ETF savers the lesson is uncomfortable but familiar. A world index such as the MSCI World is not a technology fund, yet Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet are among its largest holdings, and diversification offers little protection when large parts of the market fall together.

meldungen.titel: Berlin wants to cap petrol and diesel prices from January, but exempt motorway stations
meldungen.text:
The decision. Germany's economy minister, Katherina Reiche (CDU), has sent a revised draft law for a statutory price cap on petrol and diesel into the first round of coordination with the Chancellery and the finance ministry, Handelsblatt and dpa report. The new element: motorway service stations are to be exempt, while truck stops near motorway exits remain covered. The cap is meant to replace the current fuel tax cut when it expires at the turn of the year. The cabinet is due to adopt the law and the accompanying ordinance, which sets out how the maximum prices are calculated, on 2 December. Under the coalition's plan the cap runs for twelve months from January; the ordinance itself expires after three months unless it is renewed, and the Länder (federal states) may deviate if their procurement and transport costs differ.

The case made. The ministry argues that motorway stations have higher costs because they pay higher lease fees and are open around the clock, and that supply security comes first: "What use is a low price if there is nothing left to buy at the pump?", a spokesman said. Critics see the scheme being hollowed out. The SPD called Reiche's first draft unfit for purpose because of its high hurdles: a cap could only be imposed if German prices rose more than five percentage points faster than the EU average in three consecutive weeks, a threshold the motoring club ACE regards as practically unattainable.

The numbers. The current relief, in force from 1 October to 31 December 2026, cuts energy tax by about 14 cents a litre, roughly 17 cents including VAT. The Bundestag's research service puts the lost revenue at about 2.8 billion euros (2.485 billion in energy tax plus about 293 million in VAT), shared equally by the federal government and the Länder. A first tax cut in May and June 2026 was budgeted at 1.6 billion euros, and the ifo tracker found that only about 12 of the intended cents reached diesel drivers in May. On the motorway question, the Bundeskartellamt's Markttransparenzstelle (fuel market transparency unit) reported that the motorway premium rose during 2024 from 39 to 46 cents a litre for petrol and from 37 to 46 cents for diesel; in July 2024 it averaged 42 cents for E5. The competition authority attributes much of this to Tank & Rast auctioning fuel licences to the highest bidder.

Reality check. The claim that motorway stations face higher costs is consistent with the data: a premium of 40 cents or more exists and has a documented structural cause in the licence auctions. What the ministry has not shown is how large the cost gap actually is; a premium of that size may also reflect a captive clientele rather than costs alone. Exempting these stations therefore protects a price level the competition authority itself has criticised. The supply security argument is plausible in principle, but no published formula or cost data yet show where a cap would become unprofitable. Whether a cap is preferable to tax cuts at all, given the incomplete pass-through of earlier relief, is a value judgement as much as an empirical one. The cap's level and the ordinance's formula remain unknown.

Evidence rating: Partly grounded. The cost argument for the motorway exemption rests on a real, documented price premium, but the ministry has published no figures showing that costs, rather than market power, explain its size.
